domestications.name: Dog
domestications.blurb: Wolves that scavenged around hunters' camps became the first domestic animal, long before farming; dogs later herded flocks and guarded the first villages.

domestications.name: Sheep
domestications.blurb: Wild mouflon herded in the hills of the Fertile Crescent became walking stores of meat and milk, and later wool that clothed the ancient world and fed its trade.

domestications.name: Goat
domestications.blurb: Bezoar goats tamed in the Zagros thrive on scrub no crop can grow on, turning rough hills into milk and meat - and, overgrazed, helping strip them bare.

domestications.name: Cattle (taurine)
domestications.blurb: Perhaps 80 aurochs cows captured in the Near East founded taurine cattle; their milk, muscle and manure powered farming, while the wild aurochs died out in 1627.

domestications.name: Zebu (humped cattle)
domestications.blurb: Humped cattle bred from Indian aurochs tolerate heat and drought; they pulled the plows of South Asia and later spread their heat-hardy genes through Africa's herds.

domestications.name: Pig
domestications.region: Anatolia; separately in China about 8,000 years ago
domestications.blurb: Wild boar drawn to village waste became pigs that turn scraps into meat; domesticated twice, in Anatolia and China, which now keeps nearly half the world's pigs.

domestications.name: Cat
domestications.blurb: Wildcats came to hunt the mice raiding the first grain stores and were allowed to stay; a cat buried beside a person on Cyprus 9,500 years ago is the earliest sign.

domestications.name: Donkey
domestications.blurb: Tamed by African herders about 7,000 years ago as the Sahara dried, donkeys carried loads across deserts and opened long-distance overland trade.

domestications.name: Horse
domestications.blurb: First kept on the Kazakh steppe perhaps 5,500 years ago; the modern lineage spread from the Volga-Don about 4,200 years ago and powered war, travel and plowing until engines.

domestications.name: Camels (Bactrian and dromedary)
domestications.region: Central Asia (Bactrian); Arabia (dromedary, about 3,000 years ago)
domestications.blurb: Camels that can go days without water opened desert and steppe routes, making the Silk Road, the incense trade of Arabia and trans-Saharan caravans possible.

domestications.name: Llama and alpaca
domestications.blurb: Guanaco and vicuna became llamas and alpacas, the Andes' only large domestic animals: pack trains and wool that let the Inca run an empire without horses or wheels.

domestications.name: Chicken
domestications.blurb: Red junglefowl drawn to rice and millet fields became chickens about 3,500 years ago; over 20 billion alive at any moment now outweigh all wild birds combined.

domestications.name: Goose and duck
domestications.region: Lower Yangtze (China); later Egypt and Europe
domestications.blurb: Geese raised in a Yangtze rice village 7,000 years ago may be the first domestic birds; ducks in flooded paddies eat pests and weeds, knitting livestock and crops together.

domestications.name: Turkey
domestications.blurb: Wild turkeys were domesticated in Mexico over 2,000 years ago, first for feathers and ritual; in the 1500s Spanish ships carried them to European tables.

domestications.name: Honeybee
domestications.blurb: Egyptians kept bees in clay hives about 4,500 years ago; managed hives now pollinate crops worldwide, so farming leans on the health of an insect.

domestications.name: Silkworm
domestications.blurb: Chinese farmers bred a wild moth into the flightless silkworm, which cannot survive without people; its silk became a guarded state secret and named the Silk Road.

domestications.name: Wheat and barley
domestications.blurb: Einkorn, emmer and barley whose seeds no longer shattered needed people to sow them, and people came to need them: the bargain that built villages, cities and states.

domestications.name: Rice
domestications.blurb: Rice was being farmed in the Yangtze wetlands by 9,000 years ago; flooded paddies fed Asia's dense populations and now feed half of humanity, at a cost in methane.

domestications.name: Maize
domestications.blurb: Mexican farmers turned teosinte, a grass with a few hard kernels, into maize; now the most-produced grain on Earth, most of it feeds livestock and engines, not people.

domestications.name: Millet (broomcorn and foxtail)
domestications.blurb: Drought-hardy, fast-growing millets fed the first farming villages of northern China and the Yellow River civilizations that grew from them.

domestications.name: Sorghum
domestications.blurb: Sorghum, tamed in the eastern Sahel about 5,000 years ago, grows where heat and drought defeat other grains, and still feeds hundreds of millions in Africa and India.

domestications.name: Sugarcane
domestications.blurb: First grown in New Guinea thousands of years ago, sugarcane later drove the Atlantic plantation system and the enslavement of millions of Africans.

domestications.name: Lentil, pea and chickpea
domestications.blurb: Pulses domesticated beside the first cereals host bacteria that pull nitrogen from the air, restoring the soil fertility that grain crops drain.

domestications.name: Soybean
domestications.blurb: Soy tamed in East Asia gave tofu, soy sauce and oil; since 1950 it has become the protein feed of the world's pigs and chickens, driving land clearing in South America.

domestications.name: Potato
domestications.blurb: Andean farmers domesticated potatoes near Lake Titicaca; carried to Europe about 1570, they fueled population growth, and Ireland's dependence turned the 1845 blight into famine.

domestications.name: Squash
domestications.blurb: Squash seeds from a cave in Oaxaca are among the oldest domesticated plants in the Americas; with maize and beans it became the Three Sisters of Native farming.

domestications.name: Cotton
domestications.region: Indus Valley; independently in Africa and the Americas
domestications.blurb: Cotton was domesticated four separate times, in South Asia, Africa and the Americas; its fiber later fed industrial mills and the slave plantations that supplied them.

domestications.name: Banana
domestications.blurb: Bananas grown at Kuk Swamp in New Guinea about 7,000 years ago were bred into seedless clones; the export trade now rests on one fragile variety, the Cavendish.

domestications.name: Date palm
domestications.blurb: Date palms made desert oases livable, giving sugar-rich fruit that keeps for months; they sustained Mesopotamian and Arabian settlement and trade for millennia.

domestications.name: Cassava
domestications.blurb: Amazonian farmers tamed cassava, whose roots are poisonous until processed; carried to Africa by the Portuguese, it now feeds some 800 million people.

domestications.name: Sweet potato
domestications.blurb: Domesticated in tropical America, sweet potato reached Polynesia centuries before Columbus, and after 1600 helped fuel population growth in China.

domestications.name: Olive
domestications.blurb: Olive trees tamed in the Levant about 7,000 years ago yield oil for food, lamps and trade; slow-growing groves tied Mediterranean farmers to their land for generations.

domestications.name: Grape
domestications.blurb: Grapes were made into wine in Georgia by 8,000 years ago; wine became sacrament, currency and trade good, and vineyards that take years to bear rooted people in place.

domestications.name: Apple
domestications.blurb: Wild apples of the Tian Shan crossed with European crabapples along the Silk Road; grafting, needed to keep a variety true, spread orchards across Eurasia.

domestications.name: Cabbage family
domestications.blurb: One wild cabbage species was bred into kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and sprouts; its relatives gave turnips, mustard and rapeseed oil.

sources: Land use: HYDE 3.5 (2025) world cropland and grazing land via Our World in Data (successor to HYDE 3.2/3.3; cross-checked against the HYDE 3.2 totals in Klein Goldewijk et al. 2017, Earth Syst. Sci. Data 9: cropland 293 Mha in 1700, 578 in 1850, 1591 in 2015; grazing land 667, 1192 and 3241 Mha). Livestock head counts: HYDE (2005) historical livestock counts for 1890-1950 and FAOSTAT live animal stocks from 1961 (cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry birds), both via Our World in Data; earlier counts are reconstructions after Smil (Harvesting the Biosphere, 2013; Should We Eat Meat?, 2013) and extrapolation from population and grazing land. Biomass conventions and present-day anchors: Bar-On, Phillips and Milo 2018 PNAS (The biomass distribution on Earth: livestock ~0.1 GtC, humans ~0.06 GtC, wild mammals ~0.007 GtC, poultry ~0.005 GtC, plants ~450 GtC, crops ~10 GtC); Greenspoon et al. 2023 PNAS (The global biomass of wild mammals: wild land mammals ~20 Mt wet, marine ~40 Mt wet, humans ~390 Mt, domestic mammals ~630 Mt); Bennett et al. 2018 (broiler chickens); Barnosky 2008 PNAS (megafauna biomass crash). Crop biomass: Bar-On et al. 2018 citing Erb et al. 2018 Nature; IPCC 2006 Guidelines vol. 4 (cropland biomass defaults). Population: this project's demography.json (HYDE/UN WPP). Domestication dates: Larson et al. 2014 PNAS, Zeder 2011, Fuller et al. 2014, Piperno 2011, Todd et al. 2022 (donkey), Librado et al. 2021 (horse), Peters et al. 2022 PNAS (chicken), Eda et al. 2022 PNAS (goose), Almathen et al. 2016 (dromedary).
notes: All series are [calendar year, value] on one shared grid (-10000 to 2023; every 50 years 1700-1900, every 10 years 1900-2020, then 2023). croplandMha and pastureMha are million hectares of HYDE 3.5 cropland and grazing land (managed pasture plus rangeland, comparable to FAO permanent meadows and pastures); grazing land peaks near 3.3 billion ha around 2000 and has since shrunk slightly. HYDE's small dips (late antiquity, the Black Death) are kept. The HYDE 3.2 totals differ by 5-10 percent in 1700-1850. livestockMtC is standing live biomass in megatonnes of carbon: head counts x mean live weight of the whole herd (young included) x 0.15 carbon per wet mass. From 1900 the counts are HYDE (to 1950) and FAOSTAT (1960 uses 1961); before 1900 they are rough reconstructions. Mean weights rise with breeding and feeding: cattle group (cattle + water buffalo) ~175 kg prehistoric, ~195 kg premodern, 240 kg in 1960, ~280 kg today; sheep/goats ~23-31 kg; pigs ~30-53 kg; poultry ~1.0-1.35 kg per bird (chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys; FAO counts ~28 billion birds in 2020). horses_other sums horses (~380 kg, ~330 kg before 1900), donkeys (~150 kg), mules (~300 kg), camels (~450 kg) and llamas/alpacas (~70 kg); world horse numbers peaked near 110 million in 1910-1920 before tractors and trucks replaced them. Historical donkey and mule counts are incomplete, so horses_other before 1960 is uncertain by about 25 percent. Insect livestock (honeybee, silkworm) is tagged horses_other in the domestications list but has no biomass in the series. Present-day totals: livestock ~104 MtC (cattle ~73), consistent with Bar-On (~100 MtC mammals + ~5 MtC poultry) and Greenspoon (630 Mt wet x 0.15 = ~95 MtC). humanBiomassMtC = population x carbon per person: 0.0068 tC before 1900 (smaller bodies, more children) rising to 0.0079 tC today, which reproduces Bar-On's ~60 MtC; the ~0.009 tC/person sometimes quoted would overstate it by ~15 percent. cropBiomassMtC is the standing biomass (above plus below ground, near peak season) of cultivated plants, anchored to Bar-On's estimate of ~10 GtC of crops today (~2 percent of the ~450 GtC of all plants, after Erb et al. 2018): HYDE cropland area x a carbon density rising from ~1 tC/ha for early low-yield fields to ~2.1 tC/ha premodern (fallow-heavy annual fields plus some orchards, olives, vines and palms) and ~6.3 tC/ha today (~1.4 billion ha of annual crops at ~4.5 tC/ha, near the IPCC default of 5, plus ~170 Mha of permanent tree crops such as oil palm, rubber, coconut, cocoa and orchards at ~20 tC/ha). Averaged over the whole year, when many fields are bare, the figure would be about half. It is uncertain by roughly a factor of two before 1950 and is about 100 times the livestock value, so it needs its own scale if drawn. wildMammalMtC is wild land plus marine mammals. Land: ~20 MtC before the late-Pleistocene megafauna extinctions (Bar-On, after Barnosky), taken as ~15.5 MtC at -10000 with the American extinctions still under way, eroding with farmland expansion to ~3 MtC today. Marine: ~20 MtC until commercial whaling, falling most steeply 1920-1970 with factory ships, to ~4 MtC today. Total ~35 MtC at -10000 to ~7 MtC now, while livestock and humans rise from zero to ~165 MtC - the point of this layer. Everything before about 1900, and especially before 0 CE, is a rough reconstruction kept smooth and plausible rather than a measurement. Domestication yearsAgo are years before 2024 for the earliest husbandry or cultivation recognized in the archaeological or genetic record; many are debated by thousands of years (dog 15,000 is a conservative floor; wheat/barley and lentil are domestication-trait dates, not first cultivation; horse 5,500 is the debated Botai evidence, while the modern horse lineage dates to ~4,200; goose 7,000 is a single site, Tianluoshan, and domestic ducks are much later).
